VERDICT: ACCEPT

The counting step is correct. Isomorphism classes correspond to sorted triples $2 \le a_1 \le a_2 \le a_3 \le N$, which are multisets of size 3 from $\{2,\dots,N\}$. There are $\binom{(N-1)+3-1}{3} = \binom{N+1}{3} = \frac{(N-1)N(N+1)}{6}$ of them. Checking $N=2$ gives one surface, $\{2,2,2\}$, matching $\binom{3}{3}=1$.

The weak point is the claim that the exponent multiset is a complete isomorphism invariant. The proposed justification (automorphism groups, function fields, singularities at infinity) is asserted rather than proved. Some checks support it. For example, $\mu(2,3,7)=\mu(3,3,4)=12$, so the Milnor number alone does not separate exponent triples, but the Seifert structure of the links does. Also, for $a_1=a_2=2$ the surface is $uv=-(z^c+1)$, whose singular-fibre structure depends on $c$. I believe the isomorphism problem for these affine Brieskorn–Pham surfaces has been settled in the literature with exactly this answer, but I have not verified that result here, so my confidence is moderate.

CONFIDENCE: 3
